system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 12 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2156-11-25 20:18:00 to 2156-12-07 14:22:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with uncontrolled type 1 diabetes, nausea, vomiting, and worsening epigastric and right upper quadrant abdominal pain radiating to the back, following an inability to administer insulin due to lack of needles. Initial labs showed hyperglycemia with elevated lipase, consistent with acute pancreatitis on the background of chronic pancreatitis. She was managed with IV fluids, insulin therapy, and pain and nausea control while kept NPO. Her condition improved over two days with decreasing lipase, resolution of symptoms, and successful advancement to a regular diet. She was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to follow up with her primary care provider, continue her home insulin regimen, and maintain medication adherence.
problems: Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type I [juvenile type], uncontrolled
Dyspepsia and other specified disorders of function of stomach

17. Ondansetron 8 mg Tablet, Rapid Dissolve Sig: One (1) Tablet, 
Rapid Dissolve PO every eight (8) hours as needed for nausea.  

 
Discharge Disposition:
Home
 
Discharge Diagnosis:
Primary: Acute on Chronic Pancreatitis
         G- Tube Dislodgement

Secondary: Diabetes type 1
           Gastroparesis

 
Discharge Condition:
Mental Status: Clear and coherent.
Level of Consciousness: Alert and interactive.
Activity Status: Ambulatory - Independent.

 
Discharge Instructions:
You were admitted to the hospital for chest pain and worsening 
of your pain from your pancreatitis. For your chest pain you had 
cardiac enzymes and an EKG which was not concerning for any kind 
of cardiac problem. For your pain we gave you IV Dilaudid and we 
gave you insulin to manage your Diabetes. 
.
While you were here, your G-Tube came out. It was temporarily 
replaced with a foley until Interventional Radiology was able to 
replace your G-Tube on ___. There was concern for a problem with 
the G-tube placement/leak, so you had a CT scan of your abdomen 
which was normal and did not show any problems. 
.
Meds: 
-You should continue taking your home medications.
-You should follow up with your primary care doctor to get 
refills on your narcotic prescriptions.
-For your insulin, you should change your glargine (Lantus, the 
long-acting insulin), to 60 units at bedtime each night.  You 
should also follow the sliding scale we have provided to you.
-When taking Dilaudid, do not drive or do other dangerous 
activities after taking it.
-START clindamycin (antibiotic) for infection around your GJ 
tube, for 3 days, then stop.
 
Followup Instructions:
___

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  Epigastric pain and T-wave changes on EKG.  Question focal
consolidation.

CHEST, TWO VIEWS.

The heart is not enlarged.  There is no CHF, focal infiltrate, or effusion.
There is minimal upper zone redistribution, without overt CHF.  There is
minimal atelectasis at the left lung base.  A right Port-A-Cath type catheter
is present, with lead tip over distal SVC.  At the periphery of these films,
tubing is seen over the upper abdomen.

IMPRESSION:  No acute pulmonary process identified.  Minimal atelectasis, left
base, unchanged compared with ___.

HISTORY:  ___ woman with chronic pancreatitis status post removal of
percutaneous gastrojejunostomy tube three days ago.

Informed consent was obtained from the patient.

TECHNIQUE:  Patient was placed supine on the fluoroscopy table.  The anterior
abdominal wall was prepped and draped in a standard sterile fashion.  After
local anesthesia with lidocaine jelly a 5 ___ Kumpe catheter was advanced
through the existing percutaneous tract into the lumen of the stomach. 
Contrast injection confirmed appropriate position of the catheter in the lumen
of the stomach.  With the aid ___ wire the Kumpe catheter was advanced
into the duodenum and then into the proximal jejunum, under fluoroscopic
guidance.  The wire was then exchanged for a MIC kit catheter.  Then the track
was dilated to 12 ___ with a dilator.  Then a 16 ___ MIC
gastrojejunostomy catheter was advanced through the gastrostomy puncture all
the way into the proximal jejunum, under fluoroscopic guidance.  The catheter
was then secured with its balloon and disc mechanisms as well as sutures and a
StatLock.  Final contrast injections through the gastric and jejunal lumens
demonstrated appropriate position of the catheter.

COMPLICATIONS:  No immediate complications.

IMPRESSION:  Successful placement of a MIC 16 ___ gastrojejunostomy
catheter through the existing percutaneous tract.  The catheter can be used
right away.

INDICATION:  ___ woman with acute-on-chronic pancreatitis, recent
replacement of a GJ tube two days ago, now presents with low-grade fevers and
abdominal pain.

COMPARISON:  CT of the abdomen and pelvis ___.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT images were acquired through the abdomen and pelvis after
administration of oral and 130 cc of Optiray intravenous contrast.  Sagittal
and coronal reformats were generated and reviewed.

FINDINGS:  The visualized lung bases demonstrate linear atelectasis, new since
the prior study.  No pleural effusions or suspicious pulmonary nodules are
seen.  The heart and pericardium and the visualized portions are unremarkable.

The liver demonstrates homogeneous enhancement without focal lesions or
intrahepatic biliary dilatation.  The patient is status post cholecystectomy. 
Both adrenal glands, spleen are normal.  Both kidneys enhance and excrete
contrast symmetrically without evidence of hydroureteronephrosis or concerning
renal masses.  The pancreas demonstrates calcifications in the head, secondary
to chronic pancreatitis.  No peripancreatic fluid collections or fat stranding
is seen to suggest acute pancreatitis.  The pancreatic duct is not dilated.

The patient has had a recent revision of a GJ tube, which is appropriately
positioned with the tip in the proximal jejunum.  No post-procedural
complications or fluid collections are detected.  The stomach and small bowel
loops are normal.  Large bowel loops and the appendix is normal.  There is no
intra-abdominal free fluid or air.  The abdominal aorta is normal in course
and caliber.  No significant retroperitoneal or mesenteric lymphadenopathy is
detected.  Tiny mesenteric lymph nodes on the right lower quadrant measuring 5
mm in the short axis are unchanged since prior study.

CT OF THE PELVIS WITH CONTRAST:  The urinary bladder and the distal ureters
are normal.  The uterus and adnexa appear unremarkable with an IUD in place. 
The rectum and sigmoid colon are normal.  No significant pelvic
lymphadenopathy or free fluid is detected.

OSSEOUS STRUCTURES AND SOFT TISSUES:  No bone lesion suspicious for infection
or malignancy are detected.

IMPRESSION:
1.  No acute intra-abdominal pathology detected.
2.  Pancreatic calcifications, consistent with chronic pancreatitis, without
evidence of acute exacerbation.
3.  Bibasilar linear pulmonary atelectasis.
4.  Appropriately positioned GJ tube .

diagnoses.long_title: Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type I [juvenile type], uncontrolled

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. I’ve been having this sharp pain on my right side, especially when I walk. It comes with palpitations. And my usual stomach pain, nausea, and vomiting are still here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any chest pain or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the chest pain is on the right side, sharp, worse with walking. I’ve been feeling my heart racing a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And how about your diabetes? Are you managing your insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t taken my short-acting insulin since Wednesday. I lost my glucometer, so I can’t check my sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could explain why your blood sugar was high when you arrived—499. We’ll help you manage that here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My PCP started me on levofloxacin for my GJ tube site—thought it might be infected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We’ll continue that for now. We’re going to run some tests to check your chest pain and make sure your pancreas isn’t flaring up again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many admissions for this. I just want the pain under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll work on that. You’re getting Dilaudid for pain and insulin to bring your sugar down. We’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your EKG and first troponin were normal. We’ll repeat those to rule out a heart issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No sign of a heart attack. Your tachycardia is likely from pain or anxiety. You’re wearing a Holter monitor—cardiology will review that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my GJ tube? It’s been leaking a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep an eye on it. If it comes out, we may need to replace it. For now, it looks okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We have a problem. You pulled your GJ tube out overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t mean to. It was uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve placed a Foley catheter temporarily. Interventional Radiology will replace the GJ tube tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated. It’s a quick procedure under X-ray guidance. You’ll be fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The GJ tube was successfully replaced this morning. You can start taking oral meds again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve developed a low-grade fever and some tenderness near the tube site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan. No free air or abscess. But there’s redness, so we’re starting clindamycin just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with my penicillin allergy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, clindamycin is safe. It’s not related to penicillin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your fever is gone, and the white count is improving. The antibiotic is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My pain is better too. Can I eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re advancing you to a regular diet. You’re not using the tube for feeds, so oral intake is key.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat CT shows the GJ tube is in place, no complications. Pancreas looks stable—no acute flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s still chronic pancreatitis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with calcifications, but no acute signs. Your pain is managed with Dilaudid, and we’re limiting extra doses to one per day to stay safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want to feel in control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re letting you choose when to take that extra dose—like before procedures or when pain spikes. That way, you have some say.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar is still high—around 265. We’re worried about adjusting insulin because your eating is unpredictable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try to eat more regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We consulted endocrinology. You’ll go home on 60 units of Lantus at bedtime and a new sliding scale for Humalog.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I need to get a new glucometer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please do. Checking your sugars is essential to avoid highs and lows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin dropped a bit—from 14.3 to 11.9. We’re watching it. Could be from chronic disease or mild malnutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not acutely. It’s mild. Eating well and managing your gastroparesis will help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Pain is controlled, eating regularly, and your labs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge in a couple of days. You’ll finish the 3-day clindamycin course at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs look good. Hemoglobin is up to 12.9, white count normal, sodium improved from 132 to 136.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the rash on my arms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely not serious—maybe a reaction to a med or stress. It’s not spreading. Keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Discharge is tomorrow. You’ll go home with Dilaudid for pain, but only one pill every three hours after the first five days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I need to see my pain doctor for refills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, follow up with your PCP for that. Also, continue omeprazole, your inhalers, and the new insulin regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the clindamycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it twice a day for three days. Stop after that. No refills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. You’re alert, walking, and your pain is manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. It was rough, but I feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: take the clindamycin, use your new insulin doses, and follow up with your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And no driving when I take Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Stay safe. Call if you have fever, severe pain, or high blood sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep in touch. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before discharge. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. You’re doing well. Go home, rest, and follow the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge papers are ready. Nurse will go over meds and instructions one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you understand to take clindamycin for three days, then stop?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, two capsules every six hours for three days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And insulin—60 units Lantus at bedtime, Humalog with meals using the new scale.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll get a new glucometer today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. And call if your GJ site gets red or painful again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re officially discharged. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay in touch with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your urine was red earlier. Any more of that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not since that one time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll note it. Could be from meds or dehydration. Stay hydrated and mention it at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, you’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for evaluation of right-sided chest pain with palpitations and worsening chronic abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. She had uncontrolled type 1 diabetes due to loss of her glucometer and missed insulin doses. Initial workup ruled out myocardial infarction with normal EKGs and troponins. She accidentally dislodged her GJ tube during the admission, requiring temporary Foley placement and subsequent replacement by interventional radiology. A low-grade fever and erythema at the tube site led to a short course of clindamycin, with improvement. Pain was managed with IV Dilaudid and a structured regimen allowing one patient-chosen extra dose daily. Insulin was adjusted with endocrinology input, resulting in a new regimen of 60 units Lantus at bedtime and a sliding scale for Humalog. She improved clinically, maintained oral intake, and was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to complete antibiotics, follow up with her providers, and manage her diabetes and pain medications appropriately.
